da-2024-da-4.approach: In an undirected DFS every edge is either a **tree** edge or a **back** edge (no cross/forward edges), and an edge is classified by the direction in which it is *first* explored. Exploring $(u,v)$ from $u$ while $v$ is still undiscovered (white) makes it a tree edge — the case the official key intends.
concepts: Undirected graphs have no cross edges
da-2024-da-4.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Graph | undirected, unweighted, DFS from $s$ |
| $d[u]$ | BFS (shortest-path) distance from $s$ |
| Edge | $(u,v)$ with $d[u] < d[v]$, first explored $u \to v$ |

steps.title: Edge types in an undirected DFS
steps.body: When DFS at $u$ examines $(u,v)$ for the first time, $v$ is either **white** (undiscovered) → the edge becomes a **tree** edge, or **gray** (an ancestor of $u$ still on the stack) → a **back** edge. $v$ cannot be black: a black $v$ would already have scanned $(v,u)$, so the edge would not be explored first from $u$. Hence undirected DFS has **no cross (or forward) edges**, and "gray" is a vertex colour, not an edge type.

steps.title: Typical case: v is still white
steps.body: $d[u] < d[v]$ means $v$ is farther from $s$ than $u$. In the natural run (adjacency of $s$ = $[u, a]$), DFS reaches $u$ first: $s \to u$, and $u$ scans $v$ while $v$ is still **white**, so $u \to v$ discovers $v$ and $(u,v)$ becomes a **tree** edge. This is the reasoning behind the official answer.

scene.caption: Order 1: s → u → v — (u, v) is a tree edge

steps.title: Eliminate the other options
steps.body: **cross**: impossible in an undirected DFS (step 1). **gray**: not an edge class at all. That leaves *tree* vs *back*; the key picks **tree** — option (A).

steps.title: Caveat: a back edge is also possible
steps.body: DFS depth is not BFS distance. Same graph, adjacency $s:[a,u]$, $v:[w,u,a]$, $w:[u,v]$, $u:[v,s]$: DFS goes $s \to a \to v \to w \to u$. At $u$ the first edge scanned is $(u,v)$, and $v$ is a **gray ancestor** of $u$ — so the edge is first explored $u \to v$ yet it is a **back** edge, although $d[u]=1<d[v]=2$. The question is therefore ambiguous; the official key (A) is kept and the record is flagged for review.

scene.caption: Order 2: s → a → v → w → u, then u scans v (gray) — back edge

answer.value: **tree** edge — option (A) (official key; see the caveat in the last step)

optionAnalysis.reason: Official answer: when $u$ scans $(u,v)$ and $v$ is still undiscovered, $v$ is discovered from $u$ and the edge becomes a tree edge.

da-2024-da-5.approach: Second-derivative test: $f'(x^*)=0$ makes $x^*$ a stationary point and $f''(x^*)>0$ makes $f$ curve upward there, so $x^*$ is a **strict local minimum**. Nothing about the rest of the real line is known, so "global" cannot be claimed.

steps.title: Sign of the change
steps.body: Because $f''(x^*) > 0$, the term $\tfrac12 f''(x^*)h^2 > 0$ dominates $o(h^2)$ for all small $h \neq 0$, so $f(x^*+h) > f(x^*)$ in a neighbourhood of $x^*$: a **local minimum**.

steps.title: Why not global
steps.body: Counter-example: $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$. Then $f'(1) = 3 - 3 = 0$ and $f''(1) = 6 > 0$, but $f(-3) = -27 + 9 = -18 < f(1) = -2$. So $x^*=1$ is a local but **not** a global minimum.

optionAnalysis.reason: $f'=0$ and $f''>0$ give $f(x^*+h) > f(x^*)$ for all small $h \ne 0$ — a strict local minimum.
Only local information is given; $f(x)=x^3-3x$ at $x^*=1$ satisfies the conditions but is not a global minimum. ("Necessarily" fails.)
A local maximum needs $f''(x^*) < 0$ — the opposite curvature.
Wrong curvature and wrong scope: a global maximum would need $f'' \le 0$ near $x^*$ at least.

da-2024-da-5.shortcut: $f''>0$ → "smile" → minimum; the test is a local statement, so the answer is the local one.
pitfalls: Upgrading to "global minimum" — that needs extra structure such as convexity of $f$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
Mixing up the signs: $f''<0$ gives a maximum.
da-2024-da-5.verification: Check with $f(x)=x^2$: $f'(0)=0$, $f''(0)=2>0$ and $0$ is a minimum; the cubic counter-example shows it need not be global.

da-2024-da-6.approach: Match each access discipline to the structure defined by it: FIFO is the queue, LIFO is the stack, and key-based lookup is what a hash table is built for.

steps.title: (p) First In First Out
steps.body: A **queue** removes elements in the order they were inserted (enqueue at the rear, dequeue at the front) → (p) − (ii).

steps.title: (q) Lookup operation
steps.body: A **hash table** maps a key to a slot with a hash function, giving expected $O(1)$ search (lookup) → (q) − (iii).

steps.title: (r) Last In First Out
steps.body: A **stack** pushes and pops at the same end, so the last element pushed is the first popped → (r) − (i).

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: (p) − (ii), (q) − (iii), (r) − (i) is option **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: FIFO–queue, lookup–hash table, LIFO–stack: all three pairs are correct.
Pairs lookup with stacks and LIFO with hash tables; a stack offers no efficient lookup and a hash table has no LIFO order.
Swaps FIFO and LIFO (stack is LIFO, not FIFO) and gives lookup to queues.
Gets lookup right but swaps the stack and queue disciplines.

pitfalls: Swapping stack and queue: Stack = **L**IFO (plates), Queue = **F**IFO (ticket line).
da-2024-da-6.verification: Only one option has FIFO → queue and LIFO → stack simultaneously (A); it also has lookup → hash table.

da-2024-da-7.approach: The data are symmetric about the line $x_1 + x_2 = 0$; the max-margin separator is that line ($w \propto (1,1)$, $b=0$). Support vectors are the points lying exactly on the margins $w^Tx + b = \pm 1$, i.e. the points closest to the boundary.

steps.title: Margin for a unit direction (a, b)
steps.body: Project onto a unit normal $w=(a,b)$. Positives give $a$, $b$, $2a+2b$; negatives give $-b$, $-a$, $-2a-2b$. The gap between the classes is $\min(a,b,2a+2b) - \max(-b,-a,-2a-2b) = 2\min(a, b, 2(a+b))$, which is positive only when $a, b > 0$.

steps.title: Maximise the gap
steps.body: With $a, b > 0$, $2(a+b) > \min(a,b)$, so the gap is $2\min(a,b)$. Subject to $a^2+b^2=1$ it is largest when $a=b=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, giving gap $\tfrac{2}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$. So $w \propto (1,1)$ and the boundary is midway: $x_1 + x_2 = 0$ ($b=0$).

steps.title: Scale to the canonical form
steps.body: Take $w=(1,1)$, $b=0$. Then $y_i(w^T\mathbf{x}_i)$: $\mathbf{x}_1: 1$, $\mathbf{x}_2: 1$, $\mathbf{x}_3: -1\cdot(-1)=1$, $\mathbf{x}_4: -1\cdot(-1)=1$, $\mathbf{x}_5: 4$, $\mathbf{x}_6: -1\cdot(-4)=4$. All constraints $y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1$ hold, and exactly $\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\mathbf{x}_3,\mathbf{x}_4$ are **tight**.

scene.caption: Tight points x1, x2, x3, x4 lie on the margins x₁+x₂ = ±1

steps.title: Match with the options
steps.body: The support vectors (points on the margin) are $\{\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\mathbf{x}_3,\mathbf{x}_4\}$ — option **(D)**. $\mathbf{x}_5$ and $\mathbf{x}_6$ are at functional margin 4, far from the boundary, so they can never be support vectors.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\mathbf{x}_5=(2,2)$ has $w^T\mathbf{x}_5 = 4$, well beyond the margin; also a support set needs points of **both** classes.
Again contains $\mathbf{x}_5$ (not on the margin).
$\mathbf{x}_5$ is not on the margin; the boundary defined by $\mathbf{x}_4$ and $\mathbf{x}_5$ alone would not be the max-margin one.
Exactly the four points with $y_i(w^T\mathbf{x}_i+b)=1$ for $w=(1,1)$, $b=0$.

da-2024-da-7.shortcut: Points nearest the opposite class are the candidates: $\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2$ (distance $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ from $x_1+x_2=0$) and $\mathbf{x}_3,\mathbf{x}_4$; the far points $\pm(2,2)$ are never support vectors — only (D) avoids $\mathbf{x}_5$.
pitfalls: Picking the "extreme" points $\mathbf{x}_5$, $\mathbf{x}_6$ — support vectors are the points **closest** to the boundary, not farthest.
Forgetting that support vectors must include points from both classes.
da-2024-da-7.verification: Distances to $x_1+x_2=0$: $\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_4$ at $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.707$; $\mathbf{x}_5,\mathbf{x}_6$ at $\tfrac{4}{\sqrt2}\approx2.83$. Margin width $\tfrac{2}{\lVert w\rVert}=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$, matching step 2.

da-2024-da-8.approach: Classify each method by what it models: PCA finds a low-dimensional projection (no labels), naïve Bayes models the joint $P(x, y)=P(y)P(x\mid y)$ (generative), logistic regression models $P(y\mid x)$ directly (discriminative).

steps.title: (p) PCA
steps.body: PCA projects data onto the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix to keep most variance in fewer dimensions → **dimensionality reduction** (ii).

steps.title: (q) Naïve Bayes
steps.body: It learns the class prior $P(y)$ and class-conditional likelihoods $P(x_j\mid y)$, i.e. the joint distribution, and classifies via Bayes' rule → **generative** (iii).

steps.title: (r) Logistic regression
steps.body: It models $P(y=1\mid x) = \sigma(w^Tx+b)$ directly, never $P(x)$ → **discriminative** (i).

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: (p) − (ii), (q) − (iii), (r) − (i) is option **(C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Calls PCA generative and logistic regression a dimensionality-reduction method — both wrong.
Swaps the generative/discriminative labels of naïve Bayes and logistic regression.
PCA–dimensionality reduction, NB–generative, LR–discriminative: all correct.
Calls PCA generative and naïve Bayes dimensionality reduction.

pitfalls: Swapping NB and LR: naïve Bayes and logistic regression form the classic *generative–discriminative pair* — NB models $P(x\mid y)$, LR models $P(y\mid x)$.
da-2024-da-8.verification: Only (C) and (B) map PCA correctly; of those, only (C) labels naïve Bayes generative.

da-2024-da-9.approach: At convergence each $k$-means cluster is the set of points nearer to its centroid than to any other — a **Voronoi cell**, which is an intersection of half-planes and hence **convex**. A convex set containing $(1,1)$ and $(-1,1)$ contains the whole segment between them, in particular the midpoint $(0,1)$.

steps.title: The assignment region is a half-plane intersection
steps.body: $x$ joins cluster 3 iff $\lVert x-\mu_3\rVert \le \lVert x-\mu_j\rVert$ for $j=1,2$. Squaring and cancelling $\lVert x\rVert^2$: $2(\mu_j-\mu_3)^T x \le \lVert\mu_j\rVert^2-\lVert\mu_3\rVert^2$ — a **linear** inequality, i.e. a half-plane. Cluster 3's region is the intersection of two half-planes, hence convex.

steps.title: Midpoint of the two given points
steps.body: $\tfrac12\left(\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\right)=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}$. Each linear inequality holds at both endpoints, so it holds at their average; therefore $(0,1)$ lies in cluster 3's region.

scene.caption: Midpoint (0,1) lies on the segment joining the two cluster-3 points

steps.title: The other options are not forced
steps.body: $(0,0)$, $(0,2)$ and $(2,0)$ lie **outside** the segment, so a centroid of another cluster can be closer to them. E.g. with centroids $\mu_3=(0,1)$, $\mu_1=(0,-0.8)$ (and $\mu_2$ far away): $(1,1)$ is at distance $1$ from $\mu_3$ and $\sqrt{1+1.8^2}=\sqrt{4.24}\approx2.06$ from $\mu_1$, so it stays in cluster 3 (same for $(-1,1)$), yet $(0,0)$ is $0.8$ from $\mu_1$ but $1$ from $\mu_3$ — it goes to cluster 1. Centroids placed above or to the right similarly capture $(0,2)$ or $(2,0)$.

scene.caption: Points off the segment can belong to another cluster

optionAnalysis.reason: $(0,0)$ is not a convex combination of $(1,1)$ and $(-1,1)$ (both have second coordinate 1); a centroid below, e.g. $(0,-0.8)$, can claim it.
$(0,2)$ is off the segment; a centroid above (e.g. $(0,2.5)$) can claim it.
$(2,0)$ is off the segment; a centroid to the right can claim it.
$(0,1)$ is the midpoint of the two cluster-3 points; clusters are convex, so it must be in cluster 3.

pitfalls: Picking $(0,0)$ because it is "central" to the data — convexity only guarantees points **between** members of the same cluster.

da-2024-da-10.approach: Naïve Bayes needs the class prior and, for every class, one Bernoulli parameter per attribute (conditional independence means no joint table). Count independent parameters: $1 + 2K$.

steps.title: Class prior
steps.body: Two classes: $P(y=1)=\pi$ and $P(y=0)=1-\pi$ → **1** free parameter.

steps.title: Class-conditional likelihoods
steps.body: Naïve Bayes assumes $P(x_1,\dots,x_K\mid y)=\prod_{j=1}^{K}P(x_j\mid y)$. Each binary $x_j$ needs one parameter $\theta_{jc}=P(x_j=1\mid y=c)$ per class: $K$ attributes $\times$ 2 classes $= 2K$ parameters.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $1 + 2K = 2K + 1$ — option **(B)**. (Without the independence assumption the full joint $P(x\mid y)$ would need $2(2^K-1)$ parameters.)

optionAnalysis.reason: $2^K+1$ looks like a full joint table over $K$ binary attributes — exactly what the naïve assumption avoids.
1 prior + $K$ Bernoulli parameters for each of the 2 classes = $2K+1$.
$2^{K+1}+1$ counts a full joint table for each class (and then over-counts the normalisation) — the non-naïve model.
$K^2+1$ would correspond to pairwise attribute interactions, which naïve Bayes does not model.

pitfalls: Counting both $P(x_j=1\mid y)$ and $P(x_j=0\mid y)$ — they sum to 1, so only one is free.
Using the full joint likelihood instead of the factorised one.
da-2024-da-10.verification: Small case $K=1$: prior $\pi$ plus $P(x=1\mid y=0)$, $P(x=1\mid y=1)$ — 3 numbers fully specify $P(x,y)$, and $2(1)+1=3$ ✓.

da-2024-da-11.approach: Inserting into an open-address table probes exactly like an unsuccessful search: it keeps probing occupied slots until it finds an empty one, then stores the key there. So its expected cost has the same bound, $\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$.

steps.title: What insertion does
steps.body: To insert key $k$, probe $h(k,0), h(k,1), \dots$ until an **empty** slot is found. An unsuccessful search for $k$ follows the same probe sequence and also stops at the first empty slot.

steps.title: Same probe count
steps.body: The insertion therefore makes exactly the probes of an unsuccessful search in the current table (load factor $\alpha=n/m$), so its expected number is at most $\dfrac{1}{1-\alpha}$.

steps.title: Derivation of the bound (for completeness)
steps.body: With uniform hashing, probe $i$ hits an occupied slot with probability at most $\alpha$, so $P(\text{more than } i \text{ probes}) \le \alpha^i$ and $E[\text{probes}] \le \sum_{i\ge0}\alpha^i = \dfrac{1}{1-\alpha}$. Answer: option **(B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\frac{1}{\alpha}\ln\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$ is the bound for a **successful** search (and this option even drops the $\frac1\alpha$ factor).
Insertion = unsuccessful search, bound $\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$.
$1+\frac{\alpha}{2}$ is the expected cost of a successful search with **chaining**, not open addressing.
$\frac{1}{1+\alpha}<1$ — fewer than one probe on average is impossible, since every insertion probes at least once.

da-2024-da-11.shortcut: Insertion = unsuccessful search; the question already gives that bound.
pitfalls: Confusing with the successful-search bound $\frac1\alpha\ln\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$.
Mixing open-addressing formulas with chaining formulas ($1+\alpha$, $1+\alpha/2$).
da-2024-da-11.verification: Sanity: at $\alpha=0$ the bound is 1 probe (empty table — the first slot is free), and it blows up as $\alpha\to1$ (table almost full), as expected.

da-2024-da-12.approach: Set the gradient of the Rayleigh quotient $J(u)$ to zero. The stationarity condition is the generalised eigenproblem $S_B u = \lambda S_W u$; multiply by $S_W^{-1}$ (it exists) to get $S_W^{-1}S_Bu^*=\lambda u^*$.

steps.title: Differentiate the quotient
steps.body:
Let $N=u^TS_Bu$, $D=u^TS_Wu$ (both matrices symmetric). Then $
abla N = 2S_Bu$, $
abla D = 2S_Wu$ and $
abla J = \dfrac{2S_Bu\,D - 2S_Wu\,N}{D^2}$.

steps.title: Stationarity at the maximiser
steps.body: At $u^*$: $\nabla J=0 \Rightarrow S_Bu^*\,D = S_Wu^*\,N \Rightarrow S_Bu^* = \dfrac{N}{D}S_Wu^* = \lambda S_Wu^*$, since $\lambda = J(u^*) = N/D$.

steps.title: Multiply by the inverse
steps.body: $S_W$ is non-singular, so $S_W^{-1}S_Bu^* = \lambda u^*$: $u^*$ is an eigenvector of $S_W^{-1}S_B$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ (the largest one, because $J$ is maximised). Option **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Exactly the stationarity condition $S_Bu^*=\lambda S_Wu^*$ multiplied by $S_W^{-1}$.
Has the matrices swapped: it would mean $J(u^*) = 1/\lambda$, not $\lambda$.
$S_BS_W$ is the wrong product; the condition involves $S_W^{-1}S_B$.
No norm condition of this form follows; $J$ is scale-invariant, so $\lVert u^*\rVert$ is arbitrary.

pitfalls: Writing $S_Wu=\lambda S_Bu$ — that corresponds to the reciprocal ratio.
Imposing a norm on $u^*$: $J(cu)=J(u)$ for any $c\ne0$.
da-2024-da-12.verification: Plug back: if $S_Bu^*=\lambda S_Wu^*$ then $J(u^*)=\dfrac{u^{*T}\lambda S_Wu^*}{u^{*T}S_Wu^*}=\lambda$ ✓.

da-2024-da-13.approach: Admissible means $0\le h(n)\le h^*(n)$ for every node. Since both $h_1,h_2\in[0,h^*]$, their distance $\lvert h_1-h_2\rvert\le\max(h_1,h_2)\le h^*$, while sums, products and ratios can overshoot $h^*$ — one numeric counter-example kills each.

steps.title: Prove D is admissible
steps.body: For any node, $0\le h_1,h_2\le h^*$. WLOG $h_1\ge h_2$: $\lvert h_1-h_2\rvert = h_1-h_2 \le h_1 \le h^*$, and it is $\ge 0$. So $\lvert h_1-h_2\rvert$ never overestimates.

steps.title: Counter-example for the sum and the product
steps.body: Take a node with true cost $h^*=10$ and $h_1=h_2=10$ (both admissible, even perfect): $h_1+h_2=20>10$ and $h_1\times h_2=100>10$. Both overestimate, so A and B are not always admissible.

steps.title: Counter-example for the ratio
steps.body: Take $h_1=10$ (perfect) and $h_2=0.5$ (admissible, just weak): $h_1/h_2=\tfrac{10}{0.5}=20>10$. A small denominator inflates the ratio without bound, so C fails too. Only D survives.

optionAnalysis.reason: Can reach $2h^*$ (e.g. $h_1=h_2=h^*$) — overestimates.
Can reach $(h^*)^2$, which exceeds $h^*$ whenever $h^*>1$.
A small $h_2$ blows the ratio up: $10/0.5=20>h^*=10$.
$\lvert h_1-h_2\rvert\le\max(h_1,h_2)\le h^*$ and it is non-negative — always admissible (though usually weak).

da-2024-da-13.shortcut: Combinations that stay admissible: $\max(h_1,h_2)$, convex combinations, and anything bounded by one of them — $\lvert h_1-h_2\rvert\le\max(h_1,h_2)$.
pitfalls: Thinking a sum of admissible heuristics is admissible — only $\max$ (or a weighted average) is safe.
da-2024-da-13.verification: Table check: with $h^*=10$ the four expressions give 20, 100, 20 and at most 10 respectively; only D stays $\le h^*$ in every case.

da-2024-da-14.approach: Read the factorisation as a Bayesian network $U\to W\leftarrow V$, $W\to X$, $W\to Y$ and use d-separation. Conditioning on the **collider** $W$ couples its parents $U$ and $V$ (explaining away), so statement C is the false one.

steps.title: Draw the network
steps.body: $P(U)P(V)P(W\mid U,V)P(X\mid W)P(Y\mid W)$: $U$, $V$ are roots, $W$ has parents $U,V$, and $X$, $Y$ each have parent $W$.

scene.caption: U → W ← V, W → X, W → Y

steps.title: A, B, D: paths through W as a chain/fork are blocked
steps.body: $V\to W\to Y$ (chain) and $U\to W\to X$ (chain) are blocked by observing $W$, so $Y\perp V\mid W$ and $X\perp U\mid W$. $X\leftarrow W\to Y$ is a fork, also blocked by $W$: $X\perp Y\mid W$. All three are TRUE.

scene.caption: Observed W blocks chains and forks

steps.title: C: the v-structure is opened by W
steps.body: $U\to W\leftarrow V$ is a collider. Unconditionally $U\perp V$ (since $P(U,V)=P(U)P(V)$), but observing $W$ **activates** the path: $P(U,V\mid W)\propto P(U)P(V)P(W\mid U,V)$ generally does not factor. E.g. $W=U\oplus V$ with fair $U,V$: given $W=0$, $U=V$ — fully dependent. So C is **FALSE**.

scene.caption: Observed collider W makes U and V dependent

TRUE: the only path $U\to W\to X$ is a chain through observed $W$ — blocked.
FALSE (the answer): $W$ is a collider of $U$ and $V$; conditioning on it makes them dependent (explaining away).

da-2024-da-15.approach: By definition (Russell & Norvig), $\alpha$ is the value of the **best (highest)** choice found so far for MAX along the path, and $\beta$ the value of the **best (lowest)** choice found so far for MIN. Pruning happens when $\alpha\ge\beta$.

steps.title: What α tracks
steps.body: MAX wants the largest value, so the best guaranteed option for MAX found so far is the **highest** value: $\alpha$ only ever increases (initially $-\infty$). → (m) = highest.

steps.title: What β tracks
steps.body: MIN wants the smallest value, so its best guaranteed option so far is the **lowest** value: $\beta$ only ever decreases (initially $+\infty$). → (n) = lowest.

steps.title: Consistency check and answer
steps.body: A branch is pruned when $\alpha\ge\beta$: MAX already has a choice at least as good as anything MIN would allow down this path. This works at any depth because $\alpha,\beta$ are passed down the path. Option **(C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: β as the *highest* value would be the worst choice for MIN, not its best.
Both reversed: α would be MAX's worst and β MIN's worst choice.
α = highest value for MAX, β = lowest value for MIN — the standard definitions.
α as the *lowest* value is MAX's worst choice; pruning would be invalid.

pitfalls: Reversing the roles — remember the initial values $\alpha=-\infty$ (raised by MAX) and $\beta=+\infty$ (lowered by MIN).
da-2024-da-15.verification: The pruning condition $\alpha\ge\beta$ only makes sense with these definitions: MAX can secure at least $\alpha$, MIN can hold MAX to at most $\beta$.

da-2024-da-16.approach: "Every name in Team appears in Defender **or** Forward" means $\Pi_{name}(\text{Team}) \subseteq \Pi_{name}(\text{Defender}) \cup \Pi_{name}(\text{Forward})$; a subset test $A\subseteq B$ is written $A\setminus B=\phi$.

steps.title: Translate "or" into a union
steps.body: Names that are a defender or a forward: $P = \Pi_{name}(\text{Defender}) \cup \Pi_{name}(\text{Forward})$.

steps.title: Subset as an empty difference
steps.body: $T=\Pi_{name}(\text{Team})\subseteq P \iff T\setminus P=\phi$: no Team name may lie outside both players' relations — the shaded region "Team only" must be empty.

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: $\Pi_{name}(\text{Team}) \setminus (\Pi_{name}(\text{Defender}) \cup \Pi_{name}(\text{Forward})) = \phi$ — option **(C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Uses $\cap$: it demands every Team name be **both** a defender and a forward — too strong.
Checks the reverse inclusion (players who are both defender and forward must be in Team).
Exactly $\Pi_{name}(\text{Team})\subseteq\Pi_{name}(\text{Defender})\cup\Pi_{name}(\text{Forward})$.
Checks the reverse: every defender or forward appears in Team.

da-2024-da-16.shortcut: "Every X is in Y" ⇒ $X \setminus Y = \phi$ with X on the **left**; "either…or" ⇒ $\cup$. Only (C) has both.
pitfalls: Putting the sets in the wrong order in the difference — $A\setminus B=\phi$ means $A\subseteq B$, not $B\subseteq A$.
Reading "either … or" as intersection.
da-2024-da-16.verification: Example: Team = {a, b}, Defender = {a}, Forward = {b}. The condition is satisfied; (C) gives $\{a,b\}\setminus\{a,b\}=\phi$ ✓, while (A) gives $\{a,b\}\setminus\phi=\{a,b\}\ne\phi$ ✗.
